claim: Chromosome territories (CTs) are formed by chromosomes undergoing an elaborate folding pattern in the interphase nucleus.
source: Chromosomes undergo an elaborate folding pattern in the interphase nucleus, ultimately occupying distinct domains known as chromosome territories (CTs) (Bickmore and van Steensel, 2013; Ciabrelli and Cavalli, 2015; Sexton and Cavalli, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on chromosome territory formation.

claim: The partitioning of chromosomes into CTs limits inter-chromosomal interactions in the nucleus.
source: The partitioning of chromosomes into CTs limits inter-chromosomal interactions in the nucleus.
evidence: Draws from established understanding of CT function.

claim: CT formation has been observed across a wide range of species and cell types by both FISH and chromatin conformation capture-based techniques.
source: CT formation has been observed across a wide range of species and cell types by both fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) and chromatin conformation capture-based techniques (Bauer et al., 2012; Branco and Pombo, 2006; Cremer and Cremer, 2001; Cremer and Cremer, 2010; Pecinka et al., 2004; Rosin et al., 2018; Smeets et al., 2014; Tanabe et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Levels of inter-chromosomal contact between different chromosome pairs have been correlated with increased translocation frequencies.
source: Notably, levels of inter-chromosomal contact between different chromosome pairs have been correlated with increased translocation frequencies – both those occurring naturally in the human population and those induced experimentally in mammalian cells (Arsuaga et al., 2004; Bickmore and Teague, 2002; Branco and Pombo, 2006; Canela et al., 2017; Engreitz et al., 2012; Hlatky et al., 2002; Holley et al., 2002; Klein et al., 2011; Roukos et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior correlative studies.

claim: These correlative data support a 'contact-first' model of translocation genesis.
source: These data support a 'contact-first' model of translocation genesis (Aten et al., 2004; Engreitz et al., 2012; Foster et al., 2013; Meaburn et al., 2007; Savage, 1998; Savage, 2000), arguing that CT formation and positioning in the nucleus can influence the outcome and frequency of chromosomal translocations (Roukos et al., 2013; Soutoglou and Misteli, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior models and studies.

claim: It remains unclear if translocations are attenuated by CT formation itself.
source: However, while these correlative data support a role for inter-chromosomal contacts in directing the location of translocations, it remains unclear if translocations are attenuated by CT formation itself.
evidence: Identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The three major Drosophila chromosomes form robust CTs throughout interphase.
source: Similar to human chromosomes, the three major Drosophila chromosomes form robust CTs throughout interphase that can be labeled simultaneously with Oligopaint-based chromosome paints (Nguyen and Joyce, 2019; Rosin et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The extent to which chromosomes are packaged into CTs can be modulated in Drosophila cells by altering the activity of Condensin II.
source: Finally and most importantly, the extent to which chromosomes are packaged into CTs can be modulated in Drosophila cells by altering the activity of Condensin II, a highly conserved SMC protein complex that is essential for large-scale chromosome folding and proper CT formation (Bauer et al., 2012; Li et al., 2015; Rosin et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Oligopaint labeling of whole chromosomes during interphase is sufficiently sensitive to detect stable translocation events in the cell population.
source: Our previous work demonstrated that Oligopaint labeling of whole chromosomes during interphase is sufficiently sensitive to detect stable translocation events in the cell population (Rosin et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Preferential CT positioning in different Drosophila cell lines corresponds to stable translocations found in those cell populations.
source: We observed that preferential CT positioning in different Drosophila cell lines corresponds to stable translocations found in those cell populations (Rosin et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: BG3 cells are derived from the central nervous system of third-instar larvae and maintain a diploid karyotype with infrequent spontaneous rearrangements.
source: To determine if we could detect induced translocations that are more rare and varied in size, we turned to Drosophila BG3 cells which are derived from the central nervous system of third-instar larvae and maintain a diploid karyotype with infrequent spontaneous rearrangements (Rosin et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior characterization.

claim: Most BG3 cells recovered by 48 hr after IR in both 5 Gy and 20 Gy conditions based on a reduction in γ-H2Av staining.
source: We found that most cells recovered by 48 hr after IR in both conditions based on a reduction in γ-H2Av staining, which marks sites of DSBs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Mehrotra and McKim, 2006).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to marker validation.

claim: Neither 5 Gy nor 20 Gy IR treatments significantly altered cell viability or cell population growth.
source: Neither 5 Gy nor 20 Gy treatments significantly altered cell viability or cell population growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Translocations were efficiently produced and detected following exposure to both 5 Gy and 20 Gy IR, with 3% and 14.8% of total cells harboring a translocation, respectively.
source: In each replicate, we found that translocations were efficiently produced and detected following exposure to both 5 Gy and 20 Gy IR, with 3% and 14.8% of total cells harboring a translocation, respectively (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A few cases of spontaneous translocations were found in untreated cells (1.7%).
source: We also found a few cases of spontaneous translocations in untreated cells (1.7%).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation.

claim: Translocations between all chromosome pairs were recovered after 20 Gy IR.
source: Translocations between all chromosome pairs were recovered after 20 Gy IR, which we sub-classified as discrete translocations (mid-arm translocations where only two chromosomes were involved; 60.2%), compound chromosomes (fusions of seemingly whole chromosome arms from two different chromosomes; 32%), and complex rearrangements (resulting from multiple translocation events; 7.8%; Figure 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Approximately 33% of translocations were reciprocal with a seemingly equal exchange of genetic material between the two chromosomes involved.
source: Approximately 33% of translocations were reciprocal with a seemingly equal exchange of genetic material between the two chromosomes involved (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Different chromosome pairs exhibited different frequencies of translocations, with most translocations occurring between chromosomes 2 and 3.
source: Notably, different chromosome pairs exhibited different frequencies of translocations, with most translocations occurring between chromosomes 2 and 3 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The different frequencies of translocations between chromosomes can largely be explained by the total genomic length of the chromosomes involved (p=0.0005, r2 = 0.72).
source: As expected, the different frequencies of translocations between chromosomes can largely be explained by the total genomic length of the chromosomes involved (p=0.0005, r2 = 0.72, Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: There were variations in translocation frequency across the biological replicates for each chromosome pair.
source: However, there were variations in translocation frequency across the biological replicates for each chromosome pair.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation.

claim: Translocations between chromosomes 2 and 3 varied in frequency from 7% to 14% of the cell population depending on the replicate.
source: In particular, translocations between chromosomes 2 and 3 varied in frequency from 7% to 14% of the cell population depending on the replicate (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Factors other than chromosome size might be contributing to translocation potential.
source: This suggests that factors other than chromosome size might be contributing to their translocation potential.
evidence: Inferred from the variation in translocation frequencies across replicates.

claim: A positive correlation between the extent of CT intermixing and translocation frequency by FISH has been observed in human lymphocytes.
source: A positive correlation between the extent of CT intermixing and translocation frequency by FISH has been observed in human lymphocytes (Branco and Pombo, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: The median intermixing volume between all chromosome pairs was minimal, ranging from 4 to 8 um3, which represents ~5% of the nucleus.
source: The median intermixing volume between all chromosome pairs was minimal, ranging from 4 to 8 um3, which represents ~5% of the nucleus (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Trans interactions make up only ~7% of total chromosome contacts in Drosophila according to Hi-C studies.
source: This is consistent with previous Hi-C studies of CTs showing that trans interactions make up only ~7% of total chromosome contacts in Drosophila (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior Hi-C study.

claim: CTs are in close proximity and contact each other in 93–99% of BG3 cells, depending on the chromosome pair and replicate line being examined.
source: However, despite minimal CT intermixing volumes, our data show that CTs are in close proximity and contact each other in 93–99% of BG3 cells, depending on the chromosome pair and replicate line being examined (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Drosophila chromosomes exhibit high levels of CT contact independent of their ploidy and karyotype.
source: This is consistent with our data from tetraploid Kc167 cells (Rosin et al., 2018), showing that Drosophila chromosomes exhibit high levels of CT contact independent of their ploidy and karyotype.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Following exposure to 5 Gy or 20 Gy IR, there were no significant changes in nuclear volume, CT volume, or inter-CT contact frequencies in BG3 cells.
source: Following exposure to 5 Gy or 20 Gy IR, there were no significant changes in nuclear volume, CT volume, or inter-CT contact frequencies in BG3 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was only a weak correlation between intermixing volume and translocation frequency for each chromosome pair and replicate population (r2 = 0.16, p=0.21).
source: Surprisingly, we found only a weak correlation between intermixing volume and translocation frequency for each chromosome pair and replicate population (r2 = 0.16, p=0.21; Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: There was a significant positive correlation between the frequency of inter-CT contacts and translocation frequency (r2 = 0.42, p=0.02).
source: Instead, we found a significant positive correlation between the frequency of inter-CT contacts and translocation frequency (r2 = 0.42, p=0.02), such that higher frequencies of inter-CT contact increase the chances of translocation events occurring between those two chromosomes (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The chromosome pair and population with the lowest contact frequency overall (X-2, 92.5% contact) had the lowest number of translocations after IR.
source: For example, the chromosome pair and population with the lowest contact frequency overall (X-2, 92.5% contact) had the lowest number of translocations after IR (Figure 2H, purple arrow), whereas the chromosome pair and population with the highest CT contact frequency overall (2–3, 99% contact) harbored a translocation in nearly 14% of cells after IR (Figure 2H, orange arrow).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: A linear regression analysis predicts a 1% increase in translocation frequency for every 1% increase in contact frequency.
source: Indeed, a linear regression analysis of the data predicts a 1% increase in translocation frequency for every 1% increase in contact frequency.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Efficient translocation formation requires a high frequency of CT contact and is extremely sensitive to subtle differences in inter-CT contact frequencies across cell populations.
source: This indicates that efficient translocation formation requires a high frequency of CT contact and yet is extremely sensitive to subtle differences in inter-CT contact frequencies across cell populations.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between contact frequency and translocation frequency.

claim: Increased intermixing between two chromosomes does not predict an increase in translocation frequency.
source: Considering that increased intermixing between two chromosomes does not predict an increase in translocation frequency, additional points of contact between chromosomes do not necessarily increase the likelihood of translocation formation.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of correlation between intermixing volume and translocation frequency.

claim: Depletion of the Condensin II subunit Cap-H2 leads to a 20–27% decrease in cis interactions and a 7–17% increase in trans interactions depending on the chromosome pair.
source: Using publically available Hi-C data from Kc167 cells (Li et al., 2015) depletion of the Condensin II subunit Cap-H2 leads to a 20–27% decrease in cis interactions and a 7–17% increase in trans interactions depending on the chromosome pair (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Supported by analysis of published Hi-C data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Oligopainting of chromosomes X, 2, and 3 in BG3 cells following Cap-H2 knockdown revealed significant increases in chromosome volume, CT intermixing, and inter-CT contact frequencies between all chromosome pairs.
source: Consistent with this, Oligopainting of chromosomes X, 2, and 3 in BG3 cells following Cap-H2 knockdown revealed significant increases in chromosome volume, CT intermixing, and inter-CT contact frequencies between all chromosome pairs (Figure 3C–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The frequency of chromosome contacts by FISH was only increased by 2–5% following Cap-H2 knockdown.
source: Note, however, that the frequency of chromosome contacts by FISH is already high in untreated BG3 cells and was therefore only increased by 2–5% following Cap-H2 knockdown (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: No corresponding defects in chromosome segregation or viability were detected following Cap-H2 knockdown.
source: No corresponding defects in chromosome segregation or viability were detected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous reports suggesting Condensin II is dispensable for mitosis in Drosophila cells (Hartl et al., 2008; Rosin et al., 2018; Savvidou et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citations to prior studies.

claim: FISH-based karyotype analysis revealed no significant increase in translocation frequency or change in ploidy after 4 days of Cap-H2 knockdown.
source: FISH-based karyotype analysis also revealed no significant increase in translocation frequency or change in ploidy after 4 days of Cap-H2 knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) (Rosin et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to prior study.

claim: DNA damage was not increased after Cap-H2 knockdown alone compared to controls based on γ-H2AV immunostaining.
source: Furthermore, DNA damage was not increased after Cap-H2 knockdown alone compared to controls based on γ-H2AV immunostaining (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: CT decompaction and increased intermixing due to Cap-H2 depletion alone are likely not causal events in acute genome instability.
source: Therefore, CT decompaction and increased intermixing due to Cap-H2 depletion alone are likely not causal events in acute genome instability.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of increased DNA damage or translocations after Cap-H2 knockdown alone.

claim: DNA repair kinetics were delayed following depletion of Cap-H2 after 5 Gy and 20 Gy of IR.
source: Following 5 Gy and 20 Gy of IR, we noted that DNA repair kinetics were delayed following depletion of Cap-H2; however, similar to control cells, most DSBs were repaired by 48 hr post-IR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant changes in cell viability, ploidy, or the frequency of chromosome fragments were observed after 20 Gy IR in Cap-H2 depleted cells.
source: No significant changes in cell viability, ploidy, or the frequency of chromosome fragments were observed after 20 Gy IR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) indicating that Cap-H2 depleted cells continued to cycle following IR and chromosome breaks were undergoing repair.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The overall frequency of cells with chromosomal translocations increased moderately 48 hr post-IR with either 5 Gy or 20 Gy treatments following Cap-H2 knockdown.
source: The overall frequency of cells with chromosomal translocations increased, albeit moderately, 48 hr post-IR with either 5 Gy or 20 Gy treatments (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Chromosomes 2 and 3 exhibited a significant 50% increase in their translocation frequency following 20 Gy IR across all three replicates after Cap-H2 knockdown.
source: When analyzing chromosome pairs separately, chromosomes 2 and 3 exhibited a significant 50% increase in their translocation frequency following 20 Gy IR across all three replicates (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The translocation frequency of the X chromosome showed only a moderate increase in translocation frequencies following IR treatment and Cap-H2 depletion.
source: However, the translocation frequency of the X chromosome, which lacks a homologous partner in male diploid BG3 cells, again only showed a moderate increase in translocation frequencies following IR treatment and Cap-H2 depletion (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: DSB repair between homologous, versus heterologous, chromosomes is not increased following Cap-H2 depletion.
source: This suggests that DSB repair between homologous, versus heterologous, chromosomes is not increased following Cap-H2 depletion.
evidence: Inferred from the moderate increase in X chromosome translocations despite lack of homologous partner.

claim: In tetraploid cells with two X chromosomes, the presence of a pairing partner for the X chromosome does not reduce the frequency of X-2 translocations in either control or Cap-H2-depleted cells.
source: Additionally, in the small subset of tetraploid cells with two X chromosomes, the presence of a pairing partner for the X chromosome does not reduce the frequency of X-2 translocations in either control or Cap-H2-depleted cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: X-2 translocation frequency is significantly increased when two X chromosomes are present, consistent with the observation that translocation frequency trends with total genomic content.
source: In contrast, X-2 translocation frequency is significantly increased when two X chromosomes are present, consistent with our observation above that translocation frequency trends with total genomic content.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of translocation frequencies in diploid versus tetraploid cells.

claim: Cap-H2 depletion can increase the likelihood of forming heterologous translocations in the presence of DSBs, particularly between the two largest chromosomes.
source: We conclude that Cap-H2 depletion can increase the likelihood of forming heterologous translocations in the presence of DSBs, particularly between the two largest chromosomes.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing increased translocations after Cap-H2 knockdown and IR.

claim: The moderate increase in translocation events mimics the small increase in chromosome contact frequencies between control and Cap-H2-depleted cells.
source: The moderate increase in translocation events mimics the small increase in chromosome contact frequencies between control and Cap-H2-depleted cells, further supporting the idea that inter-CT contact frequencies are predictive of translocation potential.
evidence: Inferred from the parallel changes in contact frequencies and translocation frequencies.

claim: Increasing levels of Condensin II by direct over-expression of the limiting Cap-H2 subunit results in smaller CTs that are more spatially separated from each other during interphase in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, increasing levels of Condensin II by direct over-expression of the limiting Cap-H2 subunit results in smaller CTs that are more spatially separated from each other during interphase (Buster et al., 2013; Rosin et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Following Cap-H2 overexpression induction, Oligopaint FISH confirmed the formation of CTs that are more compact and spatially separated from each other compared to uninduced controls.
source: Following induction, Oligopaint FISH targeting chromosomes X, 2, and 3 confirmed the formation of CTs that are more compact and spatially separated from each other compared to uninduced controls (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Homologs were more frequently unpaired following Cap-H2 overexpression, resulting in two CTs per chromosome.
source: Note that homologs were also more frequently unpaired, resulting in two CTs per chromosome (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The total CT volume per nucleus was reduced compared to controls following Cap-H2 overexpression.
source: Nevertheless, the total CT volume per nucleus was reduced compared to controls (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A significant overall reduction in inter-CT contact frequencies and CT intermixing volume was observed following Cap-H2 overexpression.
source: A significant overall reduction in inter-CT contact frequencies and CT intermixing volume was also observed (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: The percentage of cells harboring a chromosomal translocation was significantly reduced from 16.7% in uninduced cells to 10.9% after Cap-H2 OX induction (p=0.02), representing a 35% reduction in translocation frequency.
source: Remarkably, the percentage of cells harboring a chromosomal translocation was significantly reduced from 16.7% in uninduced cells to 10.9% after Cap-H2 OX induction (p=0.02), representing a 35% reduction in translocation frequency (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: X-2 and 2–3 translocation frequencies were reduced by ~50% each following Cap-H2 overexpression.
source: This reduction was more dramatic when examining data from chromosome pairs separately. In particular, X-2 and 2–3 translocation frequencies were reduced by ~50% each (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: There was no significant change in the distribution of rearrangement types (discrete, compound and complex) following Cap-H2 overexpression.
source: There was no significant change in the distribution of rearrangement types (discrete, compound and complex), suggesting that all types of translocations were equally reduced (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Inter-CT contact frequencies between specific chromosome pairs and populations remained significantly correlated with translocation frequency following Cap-H2 overexpression (r2 = 0.6033, p=0.014).
source: Finally, inter-CT contact frequencies between specific chromosome pairs and populations remained significantly correlated with translocation frequency following Cap-H2 overexpression (r2 = 0.6033, p=0.014; Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: A nearly 1:1 change in the percentage of chromosome contact and translocation frequency was maintained following Cap-H2 overexpression.
source: Indeed, a nearly 1:1 change in the percentage of chromosome contact and translocation frequency was maintained.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation analysis.

claim: No significant decrease in DNA damage was seen in Cap-H2 OX cells following IR compared to controls.
source: Importantly, no significant decrease in DNA damage was seen in Cap-H2 OX cells following IR compared to controls, suggesting that the altered chromatin morphology as a result of excess Condensin II does not itself protect the cell from damage (Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: No defects in DNA repair kinetics or viability were observed in Cap-H2 OX cells compared to controls.
source: Also, no defects in DNA repair kinetics or viability were observed in Cap-H2 OX cells compared to controls (Figure 4J–K), indicating that Cap-H2 OX does not acutely impact DNA repair or cell survival within these time-points.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J-K.

claim: There was no observable increase in chromosome segregation defects during anaphase in Cap-H2 OX cells compared to controls, either before or after IR.
source: There was also no observable increase in chromosome segregation defects during anaphase in Cap-H2 OX cells compared to controls, either before or after IR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant change was seen in cell ploidy, the amount of reciprocal translocations, or the quantity of dicentric or acentric chromosomes in Cap-H2 OX cells compared to controls.
source: Finally, no significant change was seen in cell ploidy, the amount of reciprocal translocations, or the quantity of dicentric or acentric chromosomes in Cap-H2 OX cells compared to controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mitosis and cell cycle progression are unaffected by Cap-H2 OX.
source: Together, these results suggest that mitosis and cell cycle progression are unaffected by Cap-H2 OX.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of observed defects in chromosome segregation, ploidy, and viability.

claim: SLMB-depleted cells showed a significant reduction in CT contact frequencies and a > 50% reduction in translocation formation compared to controls following IR treatment.
source: Following IR treatment, SLMB-depleted cells also showed a significant reduction in CT contact frequencies and a > 50% reduction in translocation formation compared to controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant defects in DNA repair kinetics or viability were observed following IR in SLMB knockdown cells compared to controls.
source: No significant defects in DNA repair kinetics or viability were observed following IR in SLMB knockdown cells compared to controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The spatial separation of CTs driven by Condensin II activity can attenuate the potential to form translocations in the presence of DNA damage.
source: Taken together, these results illustrate that the spatial separation of CTs driven by Condensin II activity can attenuate the potential to form translocations in the presence of DNA damage.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing reduced translocations after Cap-H2 overexpression and SLMB knockdown.

claim: Chromosomes can be visualized and karyotyped for rare and varied translocations using chromosome-wide Oligo-based chromosome paints.
source: In summary, we show that chromosomes can be visualized and karyotyped for rare and varied translocations using chromosome-wide Oligo-based chromosome paints (Nguyen and Joyce, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior method and experimental demonstration in this study.

claim: Chromosome painting offers absolute translocation frequency in the cell population, in contrast to population-based methods that can measure relative translocation breakpoint usage.
source: In contrast to population-based methods that can measure relative translocation breakpoint usage, chromosome painting offers absolute translocation frequency in the cell population.
evidence: Draws from understanding of the method's capabilities.

claim: Translocation frequencies in Drosophila cells strongly correlate with chromosome size.
source: We find that translocation frequencies in Drosophila cells strongly correlate with chromosome size, and variations in translocation frequencies between cell populations can be explained by changes in inter-CT contact frequency.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study.

claim: In the presence of DNA damage, a 1% increase in inter-CT contact in a cell population yields a 1% increase in translocation frequency.
source: Indeed, in the presence of DNA damage, a 1% increase in inter-CT contact in a cell population yields a 1% increase in translocation frequency.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis presented in the study.

claim: The extent of intermixing between chromosomes does not correlate with translocation potential, in contrast to what has been observed in human cells.
source: Surprisingly, the extent of intermixing between chromosomes does not correlate with translocation potential, in contrast to what has been observed in human cells (Branco and Pombo, 2006).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in this study and citation to contrasting prior study.

claim: The discrepancy between Drosophila and human cells regarding intermixing and translocation potential could be explained by the relatively larger number of chromosomes in human cells.
source: This discrepancy could be explained by the relatively larger number of chromosomes in human cells, which would limit the probability of contact between any two chromosomes in the nucleus.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the difference between systems.

claim: In human cells, the median intermixing volume measured between each chromosome pair may be completely dependent on the frequency of their contact in the cell population.
source: In this context, the median intermixing volume measured between each chromosome pair may be completely dependent on the frequency of their contact in the cell population, with an increased number of cells in contact yielding a higher median intermixing volume.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the relationship between contact frequency and intermixing volume.

claim: Inter-CT contact frequencies in the cell population are the predominant spatial risk factor for translocation genesis.
source: This would support a model in which inter-CT contact frequencies in the cell population are the predominant spatial risk factor for translocation genesis, consistent with previously observed correlations between preferential CT neighbors and translocation frequency in a number of systems (Arsuaga et al., 2004; Branco and Pombo, 2006; Engreitz et al., 2012; Hlatky et al., 2002; Holley et al., 2002; Parada et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from experimental results and supported by citations to prior correlative studies.

claim: Using Condensin II depletion as a genetic tool to disrupt CT partitioning in Drosophila cells establishes that increasing inter-chromosomal interactions predisposes large chromosomes to increased translocations in the presence of DNA damage.
source: Using Condensin II depletion as a genetic tool to disrupt CT partitioning in Drosophila cells, we establish that increasing inter-chromosomal interactions does indeed predispose large chromosomes to increased translocations in the presence of DNA damage.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study.

claim: By overexpressing Condensin II directly or by removing its negative regulator SLMB, it is possible to enhance the spatial separation of CTs prior to IR and reduce the translocation potential of chromosome pairs by up to 50%.
source: Moreover, by overexpressing Condensin II directly or by removing its negative regulator SLMB, we are able to enhance the spatial separation of CTs prior to IR and demonstrate that this is sufficient to reduce the translocation potential of chromosome pairs by up to 50%.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study.

claim: It cannot be ruled out that Condensin II impacts translocation frequency independent from its role in CT formation.
source: Importantly, we cannot rule out the possibility that Condensin II impacts translocation frequency independent from its role in CT formation.
evidence: Acknowledges alternative explanations.

claim: Genome instability due to altered chromatin structure or chromosome segregation defects could contribute to translocation genesis.
source: For example, genome instability due to altered chromatin structure or chromosome segregation defects could contribute to translocation genesis.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about alternative mechanisms.

claim: No increased DNA damage or chromosome segregation defects were observed in Drosophila BG3 cells following either Condensin II depletion or overexpression.
source: However, we do not observe any increased DNA damage or chromosome segregation defects in Drosophila BG3 cells following either Condensin II depletion or overexpression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study.

claim: A 1:1 decrease in inter-CT contact and translocation frequency between specific chromosome pairs was observed following Cap-H2 overexpression.
source: Moreover, we observed a 1:1 decrease in inter-CT contact and translocation frequency between specific chromosome pairs following Cap-H2 overexpression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The data are more consistent with a causal role of CT organization in maintaining genome integrity.
source: Therefore, these data are more consistent with a causal role of CT organization in maintaining genome integrity.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results and lack of alternative explanations.

claim: The only method currently available to modulate CT organization is through altering Condensin II activity.
source: Considering the only method currently available to modulate CT organization is through altering Condensin II activity, further testing of this model awaits the identification of additional factors.
evidence: Draws from current knowledge of available methods.

claim: Condensin II is essential for proper CT compaction in Drosophila and yeast.
source: Although Condensin II is essential for proper CT compaction in Drosophila and yeast (Iwasaki et al., 2016; Rosin et al., 2018), it remains unclear if this function is conserved in mammals due to the essential role of this complex in chromosome segregation.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: It remains unclear if Condensin II's function in CT compaction is conserved in mammals due to the essential role of this complex in chromosome segregation.
source: Although Condensin II is essential for proper CT compaction in Drosophila and yeast (Iwasaki et al., 2016; Rosin et al., 2018), it remains unclear if this function is conserved in mammals due to the essential role of this complex in chromosome segregation.
evidence: Identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Loss of ARID1A in human cells disrupts NCAPH2 localization during interphase and leads to increased chromosome volumes and inter-CT interactions by both Hi-C and FISH.
source: Intriguingly, however, loss of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex component ARID1A in human cells has recently been shown to disrupt NCAPH2 localization during interphase and lead to increased chromosome volumes and inter-CT interactions by both Hi-C and FISH (Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent study.

claim: NCAPH2 loss significantly negatively correlated with increased inter-chromosomal interactions observed in Hi-C analysis.
